title: i-DEQ: A stable inertial Deep Equilibrium model for image restoration
claim: Our momentum-based variant trains stably where the standard equilibrium model diverges, and reaches comparable quality in a fraction of the time.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, left-to-right, shared legend colors, dashed vertical reference line
description: Two line plots sit side by side, both showing PSNR against time in seconds. The left plot uses a log time axis from 3×10^3 to 10^5 and shows training curves. The dashed blue DEQ (100) curve collapses sharply downward. The orange dashed DEQ (200) curve rises, then becomes erratic and drops. The solid green i-DEQ (100) and red i-DEQ (200) curves climb smoothly and steadily. The purple i-DEQ-P (100) curve is on top and rises fastest. The right plot shows PSNR against inference time from 0 to about 300 s, with a dashed vertical line at 60 s and dots marking each curve there. The i-DEQ curves, especially i-DEQ-P and the green one, saturate near 28.2 within about 60 s. DEQ (200) and RISP reach similar quality much later or plateau lower, and DEQ (100) stays far below. Legends sit inside each plot.
caption: Training on 100 images and inference on a test set of 20 images for DEQ-based methods on a subset of FastMRI [62]. (a) impact of the number of fixed-point iterations in the forward pass during training. Standard DEQ becomes unstable for both 100 and 200 iterations, whereas i-DEQ remains stable and shows a steady PSNR improvement. i-DEQ-P (100) exhibits faster improvement than i-DEQ and DEQ while being more stable than DEQ. (b) PSNR vs inference time for reaching the stopping criterion. i-DEQ, trained with 100 and 200 iterations, is compared to a classical DEQ with matching iteration budgets and to RISP [91]; it achieves similar PSNR 2–5× faster.
abstract: Deep Equilibrium Models (DEQs) are an established framework for image restoration that learn a problem-adapted regularization by solving a fixed-point (i.e. equilibrium) problem. While flexible and expressive, DEQs are often hindered by high computational cost and training instability. We propose an inertial DEQ (i-DEQ) that learns an explicit nonconvex regularization within the DEQ formulation. By using momentum within the fixed-point iterations, i-DEQ has convergence guarantees and accelerated rates. Moreover, we observe that i-DEQ is significantly more stable during the training and robust to rough initialization than DEQs. Numerical experiments on various linear and nonlinear inverse problems demonstrate that i-DEQ achieves reconstruction quality comparable to state-of-the-art methods, while reducing DEQ's inference time by a factor of two.
